description_full: Rengo Co., Ltd., together with its subsidiaries, manufactures and sells paperboard and packaging-related products in Asia, Europe, and internationally. The company operates through Paperboard and Paper Processing-Related Business; Flexible Packaging-Related Business; Heavy Duty Packaging-Related Business; Overseas Business; and Other Businesses segments. It offers paperboard products, such as containerboards, boxboards, tube boards, chipboards, processed paper products; corrugated packaging products, including smart display packaging, functional and decorative corrugated products, and support systems for e-commerce packaging, as well as materials for distribution, shipping, and construction; and folding cartons, comprising decorative printing corrugated packaging, and paperboard multi-packs. The company also provides flexible packaging products, such as film packaging, labels, cellophane, and preserving packaging products. In addition, it offers heavy-duty packaging products, such as flexible containers, heavy-duty polyethylene products. Further, the company provides packaging machinery, including e-commerce packaging systems, wraparound and setup forming machines, box/tray making machines, sealing machines, box opening systems, ink-jet printers, and other machines. Additionally, it offers various functional materials; sealing materials, including kraft and OPP tape, cloth tape, and hot-melt adhesive products; and nonwoven products, water-absorbent mats and sheets, cushioning mats. It is also involved in the transportation, insurance agency, leasing, and real estate businesses. Rengo Co., Ltd. was founded in 1909 and is headquartered in Osaka, Japan.

financial_summary: Rengo Co., Ltd. is a mid-cap consumer cyclical business with a $2.3B market cap on $6.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.

Returns on capital run at 3% against a 7% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and 18% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.
The company is burning through $80M of cash, and without positive owner earnings any valuation rests on hope rather than evidence.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.9× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 6.7×.

Shareholder yield of 2.3% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 17% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and profit capture is only 0.4× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.
